title: Wendell and the Atlas
premise: In 1899, Felix Kavanagh drives for the suffragist Edith Marchmont and quietly reads every letter she entrusts to him, memorizing names in a ledger of women wronged by courts, employers, and husbands. When the army requisitions their town under emergency order and seizes the ledger as evidence of sedition, Felix—half-remembered orphan, nobody's son, nobody's record—becomes the only person who can carry the truth out. Smuggling copies past three checkpoints alongside a deserter and a printer's daughter, he discovers his own name is in the ledger's final pages, written by a mother he never knew. The book ends at the century's turn: the evidence reaches London, the trials collapse, and Felix, no longer invisible, chooses to sign his own name for the first time.
about_author: Casper Iversen is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing suffrage-era correspondence in northern England before turning to fiction. He writes about ordinary people caught in the machinery of history, and this is his second novel.

chapters.title: The Weight of Letters
chapters.summary: Felix Kavanagh, driver and unofficial reader of Edith Marchmont's correspondence, introduces his habit of memorizing what passes through his hands. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: quiet pride in being unseen, shadowed by loneliness.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Small Injustices
chapters.summary: Edith reveals the ledger—names, dates, wrongs—that she and her circle have kept for years. She asks Felix to copy it, trusting him more than any clerk. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: the intoxicating weight of being trusted.

chapters.title: Orders from the Capital
chapters.summary: Emergency powers arrive; soldiers requisition the town hall, the print shop, and finally Marchmont House itself. The magistrate's men take the ledger. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: dread arriving like weather, inevitable and impersonal.

chapters.title: What the Soldiers Took
chapters.summary: Edith is placed under house arrest pending trial. Felix, dismissed as 'just the driver,' walks free—and realizes invisibility is now his only weapon. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: guilt sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Printer's Daughter
chapters.summary: Felix seeks Nell Barrow, whose father's press was seized; she has a hand-copied fragment of the ledger hidden in a hymnal. They form an uneasy alliance. POV: Felix, with Nell's account embedded. Emotional beat: wary kinship between two people with nothing left to lose.

chapters.title: The Deserter in the Boathouse
chapters.summary: Felix shelters Corporal Amos Reed, who fled rather than serve as gaoler for political prisoners. Reed knows the checkpoint rotations. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: fear transmuted into purpose.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints
chapters.summary: The plan takes shape: three copies, three routes—the river barge, the mail coach, and Felix himself on foot through the marshes—to reach a barrister in London before the assizes. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: hope that feels like arrogance.

chapters.title: First Copy, First Loss
chapters.summary: Nell's river route fails; the barge is boarded and her copy burned. She barely escapes arrest. POV: Nell. Emotional beat: grief and fury, and the terrible arithmetic of sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Magistrate's Offer
chapters.summary: The magistrate summons Felix privately—he knows about the reading, the copying—and offers immunity if Felix testifies that Edith acted alone. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: temptation wearing a reasonable face.

chapters.title: What My Mother Wrote
chapters.summary: Reconstructing the ledger from memory, Felix reaches its final pages and finds an entry in his mother's hand: his own name, his own history, recorded before she vanished. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: identity cracking open like ice.

chapters.title: Second Copy
chapters.summary: Reed carries the mail-coach copy but is recognized at the second checkpoint; he tears pages free and scatters them to the wind rather than surrender them. POV: Reed. Emotional beat: defiant ruin.

chapters.title: House Arrest
chapters.summary: Felix visits Edith under guard; she tells him the ledger was never meant to win in court—it was meant to be read aloud, publicly, so the names could not be erased. POV: Edith. Emotional beat: reframing victory as witness, not verdict.

chapters.title: The Marsh Road
chapters.summary: Felix sets out on foot with the last copy sewn into his coat, guided by marshmen who owe Edith old debts. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: solitude made bearable by borrowed loyalty.

chapters.title: Checkpoint One
chapters.summary: At the toll bridge, a young sergeant searches Felix and finds nothing—but asks him to read a letter home, unaware of the irony. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: tenderness inside danger.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Two
chapters.summary: A paid informer identifies Felix at the market town inn; he escapes through a slaughterhouse with Nell, who has followed secretly against orders. POV: Nell. Emotional beat: anger at each other becoming trust.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Three
chapters.summary: At the rail junction, the magistrate waits personally. Felix hands over a decoy bundle while the true pages travel in Nell's hymnal, sung through the barrier in plain sight. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: audacity as survival.

chapters.title: The Century Turns
chapters.summary: New Year's Eve in London: church bells, crowds, and the barrister reading the ledger's names aloud on the steps of the Inns of Court as 1900 arrives. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: awe—the moment witness becomes record.

chapters.title: Collapse of the Assizes
chapters.summary: With the ledger public and Reed's scattered pages surfacing, the prosecution disintegrates; the magistrate resigns rather than face inquiry. POV: alternating brief accounts. Emotional beat: justice arriving sideways, imperfect but real.

chapters.title: Return
chapters.summary: Felix comes home to find Edith freed and the town changed—some grateful, some resentful, none able to call him invisible again. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: belonging that costs something.

chapters.title: The Name in the Ledger
chapters.summary: Edith gives Felix the original final page: his mother's entry, and a forwarding address long dead. He grieves the woman he can only know through ink. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: mourning and gratitude entwined.

chapters.title: Signing His Name
chapters.summary: Asked to witness a new petition, Felix signs his full name for the first time—not Kavanagh, the foundling name, but the one his mother wrote. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: quiet triumph of self-authorship.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: A year later, Felix drives again, reads letters still, and trains Nell's apprentices in the discipline of memory. The atlas of small injustices continues, carried forward. POV: Felix. Emotional beat: inheritance accepted, the road open.
